topics.summary: Finding an identifier is easy until duplicates, empty inputs, and insertion boundaries enter the contract. topics.title: 15.1 Performing Linear Search
topics.summary: Linear search asks elements in sequence whether they satisfy the match condition. It requires no sorted-order promise. This simplicity is valuable when the input is short, arrives only once, or is changing too often to justify maintaining an index.

topics.title: 15.1.2 Understanding Linear Complexity
topics.summary: For n values, an absent key requires n comparisons. A match at position i requires i+1 comparisons, giving O(n) worst-case work and O(1) additional storage. The best case is constant work when the first value matches. An average-case claim requires assumptions about the distribution of keys and hit locations.

Sorted input under the matching comparator is sufficient for the needed partition. More generally, a lower-bound operation needs the predicate “element is less than this key” to be true for a prefix and false afterward. The book’s public example uses sorted vectors because that stronger precondition is easier to maintain across many different keys.

Random access lets each midpoint be reached directly. A generic library lower bound can use non-random-access iterators while keeping logarithmic comparisons, but traversal steps can be linear. Do not transfer the vector implementation’s whole cost model to a linked list merely because the function name is the same.

Exact search then checks whether the lower-bound position is inside the vector and equal to the key. A lower bound by itself is not a membership result. This final distinction prevents absent keys between values or above the range from being incorrectly reported as present.
